title: δ and θ: the two th sounds

steps.text: You already say both sounds: δ is the th of “this” and θ is the th of “thin”. What trips you up is the eye. English writes both as th, so nothing on the page tells you which is which; and δ looks like the d it is named after, so a reader says δέ as “deh” and ἀδελφός with a d. In Greek as it is spoken today δ is never a d, and θ is never the th of “this”.

Put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow, with no voice: that is θ, the th of “thin”. Now hum while you do it: that is δ, the th of “this”. With a finger on your throat you feel δ buzz and θ not. Then say “this thin” slowly: δ, then θ.
Listen for the buzz: θ in θεός and ἀλήθεια has none, δ in ἀδελφός and δίκαιος hums. ἐθεασάμεθα has two θ.
Each pair differs only in δ and θ: the hum of “this” against the breath of “thin”. The last two are one word, nothing, which the New Testament spells both ways.
Say each word after the voice. Never a d for δ: the tongue stays at the teeth and the voice hums. For θ, no voice, only breath.
Here θ comes seven times and δ twice, each marked. Hear it, then say it: breath for every θ, a hum for the δ of οἴδαμεν and δέ.
